transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-04-27
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Rina (Redwood Solutions), Samir (CinderView Infra), Leah (CinderView ML Platform), Omar (CinderView SRE), Priya (CinderView Security)

Summary:
We ran through a focused engineering deep-dive into a recent production incident where CinderView observed recurring latency spikes and token-generation stalls correlated with KV cache eviction events for long-context conversations. Primary goals: identify root causes (hot-prefix thrash vs memory pressure vs prefetch miss patterns), validate telemetry, and agree on short-term mitigations and a bench test plan for a PoC.

Topics:
- KV eviction patterns and prefix-level contention
- Paging/spill behavior when session store exceeds GPU-resident KV capacity
- Long-context replay & KV prefetch heuristics
- Batch sizing interplay with cold/hot prefixes
- Quantization/efficiency impact on memory footprints (int8 vs int4 tradeoffs)
- VPC/on-prem constraints and private deployment telemetry access

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick intro, we'll do a short recap of the incident and then go into the KV traces. Diego will drive the KV timelines.

[00:18] Samir: thanks, yea — we had the spikes last thursday, roughly 200ms additional tail latency and a few requests that hit 2s while the token stream stalled, which caused UX drop.

[00:34] Diego: ok, I'm gonna share a set of heat maps — fair warning, some of the keys in the export are obfuscated so you might see k-pref-1234 instead of user session ids.

[00:45] Leah: that’s fine. also quick note — many of our convs are long, 8–12k tokens, with frequent back-and-forth so the prefix reuse seems... inconsistent.

[00:58] Diego: right — first observation: we saw repeated hot-prefix churn where a small set of prefixes (approx 3% of active sessions) accounted for ~40% of KV evictions in the window. eviction spikes aligned with GC/compaction ops on the node.

[01:20] Omar: when you say eviction, is that in-memory evict or spill to disk? our infra shows both but we mostly saw the GPU-side kv drop and then a stall while the runtime fetched from spill store.

[01:36] Diego: exactly — in this case, the runtime triggered a spill to host memory and then to NFS (we're seeing two-tier spill). the latency jump came from synchronous fetches during generation when the model requested prefixes that had been evicted.

[01:55] Maya: and those fetches blocked the token stream because we didn't have an async prefetch path enabled in their config, correct?

[02:07] Diego: correct. your cluster had prefetching off (policy: conservative) and the batching configuration used a hard max batch size that increased token latency when prefetch missed.

[02:25] Samir: why did prefetching not catch the hot prefixes? we thought the default heuristics would pre-warm.

[02:33] Diego: so two reasons: (1) the prefetch window is time-based and the conversation pattern had bursts separated by short idle windows that fell outside the heuristic; (2) prefix keys were not consistently canonicalized; we detected prefix key variants (small metadata differences) that prevented reuse.

[02:58] Leah: that explains a lot — we do add session-level metadata (locale, client-version) into key derivation. maybe that’s the culprit.

[03:10] Priya: from security side, we salt keys to avoid cross-tenant leakage; we can't remove the salt but perhaps we can canonicalize the hashing input.

[03:20] Diego: canonicalization is doable — strip transient metadata from the prefix hash or have a stable identifier mapping. that will reduce apparent distinct prefixes and improve cache hit rate.

[03:35] Maya: can you show the timeline where the runtime evicted the KV and then a sequence of requests hit rehydration?

[03:44] Diego: yes — I'll narrate: at T+00 we have normal steady state; at T+12m the node's heap crosses the high watermark due to a concurrent background snapshot and the eviction engine starts freeing the least-recently-used slots. hot prefix A is evicted after a series of small writes from a micro-batch job. at T+12m:15s, request R-278 asks for tokens that require A; the runtime synchronously fetches A from host and blocks for ~430ms while waiting on NFS I/O; the token loop times out an internal micro-window and you see a partial stream followed by a stall.

[04:30] Omar: 430ms is huge. is that because you fell back to NFS instead of a local SSD?

[04:38] Diego: yes. the spill policy writes to a remote volume in your on-prem config and reads are subject to network latency. We also saw some stall amplification because several parallel requests waited for the same prefix and there was no de-duplication for in-flight rehydration.

[04:58] Samir: so basically thundering-herd on a hot prefix — multiple token streams all hitting the same missing prefix and each initiating a read.

[05:07] Diego: exact wording. runtime supports an in-flight request coalescing feature but you have it disabled for memory determinism. enabling it would collapse concurrent reads into one (with queued fibers waiting).

[05:25] Leah: what's the risk of enabling coalescing? we'd like determinism in tail-latency.

[05:33] Diego: coalescing increases short-term latency for the first request slightly but avoids N * read cost. tradeoff: slightly higher jitter on the leading request vs big tail reduction. in practice it reduces 95/99th latency.

[05:50] Priya: on the VPC/on-prem constraints — we are under strict compliance, we can't accept remote S3-like spill without encryption and audit hooks. how do we validate that?

[06:01] Maya: Redwood can provide the spill encryption details — AES-GCM with customer-managed keys possible via KMS/HSM integration. Diego, can you confirm the audit hooks?

[06:10] Diego: yes — we emit audit spans for spill and rehydrate ops to tracing. For private deployments we can forward to your tracing collector over mutual TLS and include an event per spill with metadata.

[06:22] Samir: good. for our bench PoC we want to force spill to local NVMe to avoid network noise and measure pure disk latency — can Redwood emulate that?

[06:31] Diego: yes, the runtime supports local-disk spill and we can provision a dedicated NVMe in the PoC harness. we'll also run a mode that simulates cold-disk (higher latency) to reproduce your production curves.

[06:45] Rina: quick question about quantization — could switching to int4 reduce resident KV memory enough to prevent eviction?

[06:54] Diego: quantization helps model weight and activations size; KV cache is primarily KV pairs (keys + cached activations). int4 reduces activation footprint but you might see slightly different numeric behavior; there are quality/regression risks. int8 often gives a good middle ground. we can run an eval with your prompt set and measure perplexity/regression alignment.

[07:15] Leah: what's the expected reduction ballpark?

[07:18] Diego: for our LLMs we've seen 30–45% reduction in activation footprint moving from float16 to int8, and an additional ~20% moving to int4, but quantization interacts with KV layout so results vary.

[07:33] Omar: any runtime knobs to delay eviction during bursty periods?

[07:38] Diego: yes we have an adaptive-thermostat for the KV residency that can hold items past high-water thresholds for a short, bounded grace period if they are high-reuse candidates. it uses a weighted hotness score. enabling it reduces evictions for hot prefixes but raises resident memory; you'd tune thresholds per node.

[07:57] Priya: does that change impact reliability or crash recovery? we need predictable OOM behavior for audits.

[08:05] Diego: it's bounded — when the grace buffer is exhausted the engine will still evict. it shouldn't cause OOMs if configured with sensible caps; we can set soft caps and alerting to notify SRE before hard thresholds.

[08:20] Maya: let's discuss the canonicalization step — Leah, can you describe the metadata you're currently adding to the prefix key?

[08:28] Leah: we append client-version, region, user-agent, and a tiny session entropy field. the idea was to isolate session variants but it's fragmenting the prefix space.

[08:37] Diego: recommended change: create a stable conversation id (sha256 of stable fields only) and keep transient metadata as tags not part of the cache key. that will drastically reduce unique keys.

[08:48] Samir: will that break any security assumptions about tenancy?

[08:52] Priya: as long as tenant isolation remains enforced at the storage level and the stable id includes tenant-id, we're comfortable. Diego, can canonicalization preserve tenant-id?

[09:03] Diego: yes. include tenant id + conversation seed; drop client-version and ephemeral entropy. do we have consent from product to change hashing?

[09:12] Leah: yes, product is ok as long as behavior is unchanged for distinct users. i'll open a PR to update the key derivation logic.

[09:22] Maya: good. next — batching. we noticed that when many sessions miss the cache simultaneously, batch formation causes head-of-line blocking. can you explain interaction?

[09:33] Diego: when the scheduler groups token-generation requests into a single large batch, and the batch contains requests where multiple items are waiting on rehydration, the whole batch stalls until the slowest item is available. smaller batches reduce stall amplification but increase per-token overhead. solution space: (1) prioritize ready fibers, (2) dynamic batch size that drops cold requests, (3) pre-scan to detect missing prefixes and route them to a separate slow-path batch.

[10:05] Omar: route to a slow-path batch sounds promising. any precedence?

[10:09] Diego: yes we have internal experiments where we separate requests by KV hit/miss status at enqueue; misses go to an async prefetch queue and are scheduled once warmed. reduces tail massively.

[10:22] Rina: are there telemetry signals we can expose to show when a request was served from cache vs spill vs remote? Leah, we'll need that in dashboards.

[10:30] Diego: runtime emits a per-token origin tag (RESIDENT | HOST_SPILL | REMOTE_SPILL). we can map those to metrics and alerts. Redwood will provide a Grafana dashboard template.

[10:41] Samir: great. 2 more quick things: concurrent rehydration de-dup and the bench plan.

[10:47] Diego: de-dup is a toggle in runtime: enable in-flight coalescing and we queue subsequent waits rather than issuing parallel I/O. for bench, we propose three runs: baseline (no changes), canonicalization + coalescing, and aggressive memory tuning + int8 quantization. each run will replay the same traffic and record 50/95/99 tail latency, eviction rates, and I/O counts.

[11:12] Leah: do we need data access change for Redwood to run bench on our private cluster?

[11:18] Maya: for private deployments we request an SSH-backed agent or a temporary bastion and mutual TLS to push traces; Diego will coordinate with Priya for security review.

[11:29] Priya: we require an IP allowlist and ephemeral keys; also want to ensure any exported traces are PII-scrubbed.

[11:36] Diego: we can redact PII at the exporter and use sampled spans only. will provide redaction logic for review.

[11:42] Samir: timeline? we want bench next week if possible.

[11:46] Maya: Diego and Samir coordinate offline to confirm availability, tentatively May 4–6.

[11:52] Omar: final question — do dedicated pools change eviction behavior?

[11:57] Diego: Dedicated pools give predictable capacity; you can reserve extra resident memory for KV or pin hot-shard replicas. They reduce eviction frequency because you control node sizing, but you still need canonicalization and coalescing.

[12:09] Maya: okay let's do a short recap and actions. we should also send a one-pager with recommended runtime flags for the PoC.

[12:16] Samir: thanks everyone, this was really helpful.

[12:20] Maya: recap: canonicalize keys, enable in-flight coalescing, run bench with local NVMe spill and three config permutations, share telemetry and SOC2/KMS details, and schedule bench next week. action owners in the notes.

[12:34] Leah: will do. thanks all.

[12:40] End of meeting.
